title: THE CHURCH LIVING IN SATAN'S CITY
paragraphs:
THE CHURCH LIVING IN SATAN'S CITY
What Jesus Said to Believers Surrounded by Darkness Will Shake Every Comfortable Christian
There are places on earth where evil does not merely exist—it feels organized.
Places where truth is mocked, compromise is celebrated, temptation is constant, and faithfulness comes with a cost.

Most believers imagine that if they had lived during biblical times, they would have remained strong. They imagine themselves standing with the apostles, refusing to bow, refusing to compromise, refusing to abandon Christ.
But what happens when following Jesus threatens your reputation?
Your friendships?
Your career?
Your safety?
Your future?
What happens when darkness becomes so normal that compromise no longer looks like compromise?
That was the reality facing the church in Pergamum.
And what Jesus said to them may be one of the most urgent messages for the modern Church.
The city of Pergamum was not merely another Roman city. It was a spiritual battlefield.
When Jesus addressed the believers there, He began with words that still send chills through the soul:
“I know where you dwell, where Satan's throne is.” (Revelation 2:13)
The Greek text reads:

οἶδά σου ποῦ κατοικεῖς, ὅπου ὁ θρόνος τοῦ Σατανᾶ
(Oida sou pou katoikeis, hopou ho thronos tou Satana)
Literally:
“I know where you live, where the throne of Satan is.”
Imagine hearing Jesus say that about your city.
Not a metaphorical inconvenience.
Not merely a difficult culture.
Not a spiritually lukewarm environment.
A place identified by Christ Himself as the location of Satan's throne.
Pergamum was filled with emperor worship, pagan temples, idolatry, occult practices, and cultural pressures designed to force believers into compromise.
Everywhere they looked, darkness appeared to be winning.
Yet Jesus did not tell them to run.
He did not tell them to hide.
He did not tell them to surrender.
Instead, He acknowledged their faithfulness.
“You hold fast My name.”
The Greek phrase is:

κρατεῖς τὸ ὄνομά μου
(krateis to onoma mou)
“Hold tightly to My name.”
Cling to it.
Refuse to release it.
Grip it when everything around you says let go.
Some of you understand exactly what that feels like.
You are the only believer in your family.
The only Christian in your workplace.
The only person refusing to laugh at the jokes everyone else enjoys.
The only person trying to honor God while everyone around you celebrates rebellion.
You know what it means to feel outnumbered.
You know what it means to feel exhausted.
You know what it means to wonder if faithfulness is worth the cost.
Jesus knows.
That is the beauty of this passage.
Before He corrected them, He comforted them.
Before He addressed their compromise, He acknowledged their suffering.
“I know where you dwell.”
Not “I heard.”
Not “I was informed.”
Not “I read a report.”
“I know.”
The Greek word οἶδα (oida) speaks of complete knowledge.
Perfect awareness.
Nothing hidden.
Nothing missed.
Nothing overlooked.
The tears nobody sees.
The battles nobody understands.
The temptations nobody knows.
The loneliness nobody notices.
Christ sees all of it.
But then the tone changes.
Because even faithful churches can slowly drift.
Even courageous believers can begin negotiating with sin.
Even those standing against darkness can accidentally allow darkness to enter through the back door.
Jesus tells Pergamum:
“But I have a few things against you.” (Revelation 2:14)
That sentence alone should make every believer pause.
Because this church was not abandoning Jesus.
They were not denying Jesus.
They were not publicly rejecting Jesus.
They were simply tolerating things Jesus refused to tolerate.
Some had embraced teachings connected to Balaam.
Others were following doctrines that encouraged compromise with the surrounding culture.
The danger was not open rebellion.
The danger was gradual accommodation.
The same danger facing countless churches today.
A little compromise here.
A little silence there.
A little adjustment to fit cultural expectations.
A little less conviction.
A little less truth.
A little less repentance.
Until eventually people still use the name of Jesus while no longer following the Jesus of Scripture.
The story of Balaam reaches back into the Hebrew Scriptures.
The Hebrew name is:

בִּלְעָם
(Bil'am)
His story reveals a terrifying reality.
A man can speak God's words while secretly loving the rewards of compromise.
A person can look spiritual while slowly drifting from obedience.
A ministry can appear successful while becoming disconnected from holiness.
Jesus was not warning Pergamum because He hated them.
He was warning them because He loved them.
The warning itself was grace.
That is the pattern of the Gospel.
God exposes what He intends to heal.
He confronts what He intends to restore.
He reveals what He intends to redeem.
Because Jesus is not interested in managing appearances.
He transforms hearts.
And that truth becomes even more powerful when we remember who was receiving this letter.
These believers lived where Satan's throne was.
Yet Jesus still called them His church.
Think about that.
They were not perfect.
They struggled.
Some had compromised.
Some had drifted.
Some needed repentance.
Yet Jesus had not abandoned them.
Because grace is not given to perfect people.
Grace is given to repentant people.
That is why the theme of Scripture is not perfection.
It is redemption.
From Genesis to Revelation, God specializes in rewriting stories.
Abraham lied.
Jacob deceived.
Moses killed.
David committed adultery.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted believers.
Yet grace rewrote every one of their stories.
The Gospel is not the story of good people becoming slightly better.
The Gospel is the story of dead people being made alive.
The Greek word for repentance is:

μετάνοια
(metanoia)
A change of mind resulting in a transformed life.
Not guilt.
Not shame.
Not self-hatred.
Transformation.
Turning toward Christ.
And that invitation still stands today.
Perhaps you feel like Pergamum.
Surrounded by darkness.
Surrounded by pressure.
Surrounded by temptation.
Maybe compromise has already crept into places you never expected.
Maybe you've grown comfortable with things that once convicted you.
Maybe you've become exhausted from standing alone.
Hear the voice of Jesus again.
“I know where you dwell.”
He knows your battle.
He knows your environment.
He knows your pain.
And He knows your future.
The same Savior who walked among the churches in Revelation still walks among His people today.
The same Christ who confronted compromise still extends mercy.
The same King who called sinners to repentance still welcomes prodigals home.
Because the Gospel has always been about scandal transformed into grace.
The cross itself looked like history's greatest scandal.
The Son of God mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
Yet what appeared to be defeat became the greatest victory the world has ever known.
The empty tomb forever declared that God writes better endings than humanity expects.
That is why no story is beyond redemption.
No failure is beyond grace.
No sinner is beyond forgiveness.
No church is beyond restoration.
No life is beyond transformation.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Someone living in their own version of Pergamum may need this message more than you realize.
Because one share can reach a struggling believer.
One comment can start a testimony.
And one surrendered life can become another story rewritten by grace.
The most dangerous place is not Satan's city—it is a heart that no longer listens when Jesus speaks.
